From Python (psa) to SLA > Ownership and Memory Safety

Ownership and Memory Safety

The previous pages translated syntax. This page translates ownership — the place where psa and SLA differ most, and where the difference is worth the most. psa values are dynamic and reference-like: assignment aliases, functions receive the caller's objects, release is automatic and invisible. SLA values are owned: assignment moves a non-copy value, a function parameter receives the callee's own handle unless the call site visibly lends one with &, release is an explicit, compile-time-tracked event (!x), and the type checker remembers which names have been consumed. The nine examples below are the classic psa/Python hazards — silent aliasing, use after move, double release, iterator invalidation, out-of-bounds reads, integer overflow, the mutable default argument, closure late binding, and None misuse — each shown as the psa original, the direct SLA translation, what the SLA toolchain actually does with it (measured, verbatim where quoted), and the safe form. Method, as on the earlier pages: every SLA program was compiled and run on the stated toolchain before being written down; the negative examples are judged by sla check (exit code 1), each with its corrected version as the control (check exit code 0); the psa side follows the syntax census and Python semantics and was not run locally.

1. Use After Move: the Alias That Isn't

In psa, b = a binds a second name to the same list. Both names stay usable, and a mutation through one is visible through the other — the standard source of "spooky action" bugs in Python code. The direct SLA translation moves instead, and the checker refuses the second use:

psaSLA (direct translation)
a = [10, 20]
b = a            # alias, not a copy
b.append(30)
print(len(a))    # 3 — a changed too
print(len(b))    # 3
 
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let xs: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    xs.push(10);
    let ys = xs;
    println("{}", len(ys));
    println("{}", len(xs));
    return 0;
}

sla check rejects it (exit code 1), verbatim:

Type Check Error: failed to verify types: UseAfterMove: identifier `xs` was already consumed (error.UseAfterMove)

The safe form reads whatever the caller still needs before the move — the move itself is the last use of the old name:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let xs: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    xs.push(10);
    xs.push(20);
    let n = len(xs) as i32;
    let ys = xs;
    println("{}", n);
    println("{}", len(ys));
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): 2, 2, exit code 0. There is no second owner to alias: after let ys = xs;, xs is consumed, and the checker — not a runtime test — is what says so.

2. Aliasing Mutation: a Function Cannot Silently Grow Your List

The psa function below mutates its caller's list. Nothing at the call site says so; the caller finds out by observing the damage. The direct SLA translation compiles — and then does something more interesting than erroring: the callee pushes successfully onto its own handle (length 3 inside the function), and the caller's Vec is unchanged (length 2 after the call). A by-value parameter is the callee's own handle, not an alias of the caller's value, so the silent-alias semantics simply do not exist:

psaSLA (direct translation)
def add_one(xs):
    xs.append(99)

xs = [10, 20]
add_one(xs)
print(len(xs))   # 3 — the caller's
                 # list grew, silently
 
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn add_one(v: Vec<i32>) {
    v.push(99);
    println("{}", len(v));
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let xs: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    xs.push(10);
    xs.push(20);
    add_one(xs);
    println("{}", len(xs));
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): 3 (inside the callee), 2 (the caller afterwards), exit code 0 — the push landed on the callee's handle and was gone when the function returned. If the mutation is intended, SLA makes the caller say so at the call site, with an explicit lend (&), or by taking the value back as the function's return. The lend form:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn add_one(v: &Vec<i32>) {
    v.push(99);
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let xs: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    xs.push(10);
    xs.push(20);
    add_one(&xs);
    println("{}", len(xs));
    println("{}", xs[2]);
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): 3, 99, exit code 0. The difference from psa is not that mutation is impossible — it is that add_one(&xs) shows the lend, while add_one(xs) provably cannot touch the caller's value.

3. Double Release: Freed Twice Is a Compile Error

psa releases values automatically; there is no spelling for "free this now", and closing a Python object twice is silently harmless. The bug class appears the moment release becomes explicit — a cleanup path that runs twice over the same owned handle is a double free in any manually managed translation. SLA spells early release as !x, and the checker tracks it as a consumption:

psaSLA (direct translation)
# release is automatic; a second
# cleanup pass over the same object
# is harmless — and invisible:
data = load()
close(data)
close(data)      # no error, no trace
 
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let xs: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    xs.push(10);
    !xs;
    !xs;
    println("done");
    return 0;
}

sla check rejects the second release (exit code 1), verbatim:

Type Check Error: failed to verify types: checkStmt failed at node tag release_stmt (error.UseAfterMove)

Reading the value after a single release draws the named form of the same diagnostic (also verified): UseAfterMove: identifier `xs` was already consumed (error.UseAfterMove). The safe form releases exactly once — and in most code releases not at all, letting the end of the scope do it:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let xs: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    xs.push(10);
    !xs;
    println("done");
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): done, exit code 0. What is a runtime heap corruption in a manual translation is a one-line diagnostic here, before the program exists.

4. Iterator Invalidation: There Is No Iterator to Invalidate

Iterating a psa list while appending to it is a silent logic error: the iterator is index-based, so the appended items are visited too, and a loop written against the "original" list may never finish (the dict form of the same mistake raises RuntimeError in Python). The direct SLA translation does not compile — a Vec is not an iterable value in that form:

psaSLA (direct translation)
xs = [1, 2, 3]
for x in xs:
    xs.append(x * 10)
    # appended items are visited
    # too — the loop outgrows
    # the list it was written for
 
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let xs: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    xs.push(1);
    xs.push(2);
    xs.push(3);
    for x in xs {
        xs.push(x * 10);
    }
    println("{}", len(xs));
    return 0;
}

sla check rejects it (exit code 1), verbatim:

Type Check Error: failed to verify types: for iterable value must be array or implement Iterable: start tag=user_defined (error.TypeMismatch)

SLA iteration over a Vec is an index loop, and the safe form reads the bound once, up front — pushes inside the loop then cannot extend the iteration:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let xs: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    xs.push(1);
    xs.push(2);
    xs.push(3);
    let n = len(xs) as i32;
    for i in 0..n {
        xs.push(xs[i] * 10);
    }
    println("{}", len(xs));
    println("{}", xs[3]);
    println("{}", xs[5]);
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): 6, 10, 30, exit code 0 — exactly the three original elements were processed. (The corresponding trap survives in a while i < len(xs) loop, which re-reads the length every iteration; the range form is the shape that fixes the bound.)

5. Out-of-Bounds Indexing: a Loud Panic, Never a Silent Overrun

psa catches this — at runtime, when the line is reached, with an uncatchable panic (code 77050, as page 06 showed). The honest SLA measurement is in between the two stereotypes: indexing is not checked at compile time (a literal index and a computed index both pass sla check), but the read is bounds-checked at runtime and aborts loudly. The C outcome — silently reading past the buffer into adjacent memory — does not exist:

psaSLA
a = [10, 20, 30]
print(a[10])
# runtime panic 77050 — loud,
# but only when this line runs
 
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let xs: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    xs.push(10);
    xs.push(20);
    xs.push(30);
    println("{}", xs[10]);
    return 0;
}

Verified behaviour (SLA): compiles cleanly; at runtime prints nothing and aborts with PANIC: code=32, exit code 160. A dynamic index (xs[len(xs)]) behaves identically — verified separately. The safe form checks the bound before the read, making the missing case ordinary control flow:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let xs: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    xs.push(10);
    xs.push(20);
    xs.push(30);
    let i = 10;
    if i < len(xs) as i32 {
        println("{}", xs[i]);
    } else {
        println("missing");
    };
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): missing, exit code 0.

6. Integer Overflow: Where SLA Is the Looser Side — Guard It

Python integers never overflow, and psa's i64 integers fail loudly on overflow (census; panic 77080). SLA splits the two cases, and only one of them is safe by default. A literal that fits no integer type at all is rejected by the parser, verbatim (probe file name and line numbers as emitted):

Syntax Error: failed to parse t14_literal_i64_over.sla:5:37: error.InvalidCharacter
  |
    3 | 
    4 | fn main() -> i32 {
    5 |     let x: i64 = 9223372036854775808;
      |                                     ^ found ';', expected valid character or literal
    6 |     println("{}", x);
    7 |     return 0;

But arithmetic overflow at runtime wraps silently (two's complement), measured:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let x: i64 = 9223372036854775807;
    let y = x + 1;
    println("{}", y < 0);
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): true, exit code 0 — the sum wrapped to the negative end with no diagnostic. This page does not pretend otherwise: where psa refuses loudly, SLA wraps, so the safe conversion is an explicit checked operation that returns Option (or exact arithmetic via the standard library's bigint, landed as substrate item S4):

@import "sa_std/core/option.sa"
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn checked_add(a: i64, b: i64) -> Option<i64> {
    if b > 0 && a > 9223372036854775807 - b {
        return Option::None;
    };
    return Option::Some(a + b);
}

fn or_zero(o: Option<i64>) -> i64 {
    let r = match o {
        Some(v) => { v },
        None => { 0 },
    };
    return r;
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let m: i64 = 9223372036854775807;
    println("{}", or_zero(checked_add(m, 1)));
    println("{}", or_zero(checked_add(40, 2)));
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): 0 (the overflowing add, mapped to the fallback), 42, exit code 0.

7. The Mutable Default Argument: the Construct Does Not Exist

Python's most famous logic trap: a mutable default is created once and shared by every call that omits it, so the "fresh" accumulator is not fresh. psa inherits the semantics (defaults are supported, census). SLA has no default parameter values at all, and the parser says so — with the sanctioned replacement named in the diagnostic itself:

psaSLA (direct translation)
def collect(item, acc=[]):
    acc.append(item)
    return acc

collect(1)
print(len(collect(2)))  # 2 — the
                 # default was shared
 
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn collect(item: i32, acc: Vec<i32> = Vec::new()) -> Vec<i32> {
    acc.push(item);
    return acc;
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let a = collect(1);
    println("{}", len(a));
    return 0;
}

sla check rejects it (exit code 1), verbatim:

Syntax Error: failed to parse t16_default_param.sla:5:37: error.SyntaxError
  |
    3 | @import "sa_std/vec.sa"
    4 | 
    5 | fn collect(item: i32, acc: Vec<i32> = Vec::new()) -> Vec<i32> {
      |                                     ^ found '=', expected r_paren (default parameter values such as `= 1` are not supported; define f_default() + f_full(...) instead, see demos/basic/47_default_args)
    6 |     acc.push(item);
    7 |     return acc;

The safe form makes the accumulator the caller's explicit state, lent per call. Sharing now happens only where the caller visibly lends the same Vec twice — and a fresh Vec starts empty, as the third line shows:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/vec.sa"

fn collect(item: i32, acc: &Vec<i32>) {
    acc.push(item);
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let acc: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    collect(1, &acc);
    println("{}", len(acc));
    collect(2, &acc);
    println("{}", len(acc));
    let fresh: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    collect(9, &fresh);
    println("{}", len(fresh));
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): 1, 2, 1, exit code 0.

8. Closure Late Binding: a Trap Both Languages Share

Python closures capture variables, not values: closures created in a loop all see the loop variable's final value — the classic [2, 2, 2] surprise. Measured honestly, SLA is the same: closures capture by reference, and no diagnostic is issued. The minimal pair:

psaSLA
fns = []
for i in range(3):
    fns.append(lambda: i)
print([f() for f in fns])
# [2, 2, 2] — every closure
# sees the final i
 
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let i = 0;
    let f = || i;
    i = 5;
    println("{}", f());
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): 5, exit code 0 — the closure read the variable's current value, not the value at creation. The fix is also the same shape as Python's (bind the value, there as a default argument, here as a fresh binding the closure captures instead):

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let i = 0;
    let j = i;
    let f = || j;
    i = 5;
    println("{}", f());
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): 0, exit code 0. This page lists the example precisely because it does not become a compile error: ownership checking does not repeal late binding, and a faithful conversion guide has to say which traps survive translation.

9. None Misuse: Refused by the Type Checker

In psa, None is a value that flows anywhere; the failure surfaces at the use site, at runtime, far from where the None entered. In SLA the absence is in the type, so the same program is refused before it exists:

psaSLA (direct translation)
def bump(opt):
    return opt + 1

print(bump(None))
# runtime TypeError at the use
# site — nothing flagged where
# None was passed in
 
@import "sa_std/core/option.sa"
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let o: Option<i32> = Option::None;
    println("{}", o + 1);
    return 0;
}

sla check rejects it (exit code 1), verbatim:

Type Check Error: failed to verify types: binary expression type mismatch: op=add, left tag=user_defined, right tag=primitive (error.TypeMismatch)

Even the explicit escape hatch fails loudly rather than silently: o.unwrap() on a None aborts at runtime with PANIC[17]: called Option::unwrap() on a None value (exit code 145, verified) — at the exact site, with the cause in the message. The safe form supplies the fallback as data:

@import "sa_std/core/option.sa"
@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"

fn main() -> i32 {
    let o: Option<i32> = Option::None;
    println("{}", o.unwrap_or(0) + 1);
    let p: Option<i32> = Option::Some(41);
    println("{}", p.unwrap_or(0) + 1);
    return 0;
}

Verified output (SLA): 1, 42, exit code 0.

Key Points of This Page

  • Assignment moves: a second owner cannot exist, so use-after-move and double release are compile errors (error.UseAfterMove), verified by sla check against their corrected controls.
  • Mutation across a call is explicit: a by-value parameter cannot touch the caller's value (verified — the caller's length is unchanged); the call site shows a lend (&) or takes the value back as a return.
  • There are no iterator values over a Vec to invalidate; the index-loop form fixes its bound once, up front.
  • Out-of-bounds indexing is a runtime bounds check (PANIC: code=32), not a compile error and never a silent overrun; the guarded form makes the missing case control flow.
  • Two hazards survive translation and are named as such: runtime integer overflow wraps (guard with a checked operation or bigint), and closures bind late (capture a fresh binding). A literal beyond every integer type is a parse error.
  • None misuse is a type error (error.TypeMismatch); unwrap() on None aborts loudly (PANIC[17]) at the site.
